text: Chadwell O'Connor (October 9, 1914 – September 5, 2007) was an American inventor and steam engine enthusiast best known for inventing an improved fluid-damped tripod head with counterbalance and adjustable drag, for which he won Academy Awards in 1975 and 1992. He came from a distinguished family; his father, Johnson O'Connor, was a prominent psychometrician and pioneer in aptitude testing, and his mother died when he was young; his father later remarried Eleanor Manning, an MIT-trained architect and educator. The family lived in Boston, and O'Connor often visited his father at the General Electric factory in Lynn, Massachusetts, where he developed an interest in engineering. He earned a degree in mechanical engineering from the Stevens Institute of Technology and the California Institute of Technology. Shortly after graduating, World War II began, and O'Connor joined Douglas Aircraft, where he managed aircraft production and repair. After the war, he became chief engineer at Pasadena Power and Light, where his early interest in steam engines helped improve power production and incineration. In 1974, he developed the O'Connor Rotary Combustor to burn municipal garbage for steam power generation; a pilot plant was built in Japan, and in 1980, a production facility in Gallatin, Tennessee, burned 200 short tons (179 long tons; 181 t) of municipal waste daily. This technology was spun out of O'Connor Engineering to a separate company later acquired by Westinghouse. O'Connor was deeply fascinated by steam locomotives, recognizing them as a dying breed, and began photographing them. He later refurbished and reproduced classic steam locomotives, owning an 1891 0-4-0 locomotive from 1952 to 1967. With his company, O'Connor Engineering Laboratories, he recreated the Union Pacific No. 119 and Central Pacific Jupiter locomotives, which were used in the driving of the Golden Spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, and have operated at the Golden Spike National Historic Site since May 10, 1979. Disney animator Ward Kimball painted the artwork on the No. 119. In later years, O'Connor maintained a steamboat that he operated in Newport Beach, California. In the 1990s, the O'Connors donated one of their steam engines to the Minnesota Transportation Museum for the restoration of the streetcar steamboat Minnehaha, which returned to service as a working museum in 1996 and continues to offer historic steamboat cruises on Lake Minnetonka, Minnesota. His interest in photographing steam locomotives led to the invention of the improved tripod head, which he developed to solve the jerky motion in photos of moving trains by creating a silicone-filled platform between the tripod and camera for smooth panning and tilting. He shot over 100,000 feet of film during the waning days of steam locomotives. In 1952, while filming near Glendale, California, he met Walt Disney, a fellow steam enthusiast, who was impressed by the tripod head and asked O'Connor to produce more. O'Connor agreed, building them in his garage. At the time, Disney was filming The Living Desert, one of his first nature studies, and needed smooth shots of moving animals; the O'Connor head was so effective that Disney ordered 10 more, and the film won the first Academy Award for Documentary Feature in 1953. O'Connor founded a part-time business in 1952 to manufacture the heads, and by 1969, the business was so successful that he left the power company to work full-time on camera heads and steam engines at O'Connor Engineering. He and Disney maintained a lifelong friendship and business relationship, with O'Connor designing the power systems for the steam launches and paddlewheelers at Disney World in Florida. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences awarded O'Connor a Scientific and Engineering Award (Class II) in 1975 and an Award of Merit in 1992 for the concept and engineering of the fluid-damped camera head. Throughout his life, O'Connor received 29 U.S. patents. Chadwell O'Connor died on September 5, 2007.
